prompt.context: Our client is Wildcat Wings, the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, the CEO flew with our primary competitor, Phoenix Air, and she noticed something interesting: Phoenix has stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and they now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of Wildcat Wings wants to know: (1) Why did Phoenix Air switch to card-only in-flight payments? and (2) Should Wildcat Wings follow them and switch to card-only for in-flight food and beverage purchases?

clarifying_info.q: Do all passengers on a Wildcat flight have a credit card available?
clarifying_info.a: Roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, so effectively all consumers on the airplane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: What types of items are sold on Wildcat flights?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on Wildcat flights.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other airline made this switch besides Phoenix Air?
clarifying_info.a: Phoenix is the only airline that has made the switch so far; however, all other airlines are evaluating it.

clarifying_info.q: Are Phoenix and Wildcat Wings similar in size and operations?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, Phoenix and Wildcat should be considered to be exactly the same in all regards.

exhibits.title: Flight Economics
exhibits.shows: A table summarizing key fleet and flight statistics including fleet size, aircraft type, total seats per flight, cabin breakdown by class, traveler type mix, seat utilization rates, purchase rates by traveler type, average purchase values, and current split of payment method (cash vs. card).

exhibits.title: Cash and Credit Card Management Processes
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side process flow diagrams: the Wildcat Wings Cash Management Process and the Wildcat Wings Credit Card Process. The cash process involves on-ground cash handlers, in-flight cash collection, flight lockboxes, an onsite cash processing center, an armored car service for reconciliation and counterfeit checks, with a 2% fee and 31-day end-to-end processing time. The card process involves in-flight card swipes on a wireless terminal and a merchant service, with a 2% fee and 24-hour end-to-end processing time. Additional info lists 5 cash handlers per airport and 2 employees at the onsite cash processing center at each airport.

framework: Revenue changes: estimate lost revenue from cash-only customers who will not switch to card vs. any potential revenue uplift from faster transactions

Cost changes: elimination of cash management overhead costs vs. incremental credit card processing fees (note both cash and card carry a 2% fee, so fee impact is a wash; focus on eliminated overhead headcount)
Cash flow and working capital changes: time value of money benefit from receiving payment 30 days sooner; elimination of $50/flight in change float; reduction in cash theft and damage losses
Qualitative / strategic considerations: customer satisfaction, competitive positioning, operational simplicity

questions.prompt: Calculate the total in-flight food and beverage revenue on an average Wildcat Wings flight, and the current split between cash and card payments.
questions.guidance: Candidate should methodically calculate passenger counts by segment, apply purchase rates and average values, then split by payment method. Key steps: First Class business passengers = 200 x 25% x 100% x 100% = 50; Economy business = 200 x 75% x 80% x 50% = 60; Economy leisure = 200 x 75% x 80% x 50% = 60. Business spend = (50+60) x 40% x $10 = $440. Leisure spend = 60 x 25% x $5 = $75. Total = $515. Cash = $515 x 20% = $103. Card = $515 x 80% = $412.

math.setup: Segment passengers, apply purchase rate and average spend, then split by payment method.
steps: First Class passengers: 200 seats x 25% share x 100% utilization x 100% business = 50 passengers
Economy business: 200 x 75% x 80% x 50% = 60 passengers
Economy leisure: 200 x 75% x 80% x 50% = 60 passengers
Business traveler spend: (50 + 60) x 40% purchase rate x $10 avg = $440
Leisure traveler spend: 60 x 25% purchase rate x $5 avg = $75
math.answer: Total per-flight food & beverage revenue = $515; Cash portion = $103; Card portion = $412.

questions.prompt: If Wildcat Wings goes card-only, how much revenue would it lose? Assume 1/3 of cash-paying customers will not switch and will simply not purchase.
questions.guidance: Candidate applies the 1/3 assumption to cash revenue. Lost revenue = 1/3 x $103 ≈ $35 per flight. A strong candidate will note this is a TOP-LINE loss, not a bottom-line loss, so the actual profit impact depends on margins.

math.setup: Apply the 1/3 cash-customer attrition rate to the $103 cash revenue figure.
steps: Fraction of cash customers who will not switch = 1/3
math.answer: Approximately $35 in lost revenue per flight.

questions.prompt: Analyze the cost impact of switching to card-only using the process exhibit. What overhead savings can be realized?
questions.guidance: Candidate should notice: (1) Both cash and card carry a 2% fee, so fee savings are a wash. (2) The cash management process requires 5 cash handlers + 2 cash processing center employees = 7 total employees per airport, all of which can be eliminated. The interviewer will confirm that eliminating this overhead saves $35 per flight. Candidate should highlight that cost savings go straight to the bottom line (profit) while the revenue loss is top-line — making the switch financially equivalent at first glance but actually favorable in profit terms.

math.setup: Compare 2% fee on cash vs. 2% fee on card; then quantify headcount savings.
steps: Cash management fee: 2% of $103 cash revenue ≈ $2 (same rate as card — a wash)
Overhead eliminated: 5 cash handlers + 2 cash processing center employees = 7 FTEs per airport
Net financial impact per flight: -$35 revenue loss + $35 cost savings = $0 on surface, but $35 cost savings drops to profit vs. $35 revenue loss which only partially drops to profit
math.answer: Fee impact is a wash. Overhead savings = $35/flight. Revenue loss = $35/flight. The switch is favored because savings are bottom-line while revenue losses are top-line.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the direct financial calculation, what are the additional benefits of switching to card-only in-flight payments?

categories.name: Time Value of Money
ideas: Receive payment 30 days sooner (24 hours vs. 31 days end-to-end)
Cash freed up can be invested in interest-earning accounts
Cash freed up can fund growth projects
Early payment to suppliers to capture early-payment discounts
Faster paydown of lines of credit and debt

categories.name: Working Capital Improvement
ideas: Eliminate $50 per flight in change float loaded onto each plane
Reduce losses from cash theft by flight attendants or passengers
Reduce losses from counterfeit bills
Reduce losses from cash damage

categories.name: Customer Experience
ideas: Faster transaction speed benefits the majority of card-paying customers
Reduced queue frustration may increase purchase conversion rates
Passengers at the back of the plane less likely to abandon purchases
Psychological effect: card-only removes cash-guilt, potentially increasing average spend

categories.name: Operational Simplicity
ideas: Fewer moving parts in the payment process (no lockboxes, armored cars, cash centers)
Reduced risk of human error in cash counting and reconciliation
Flight attendants can focus more on service rather than cash handling
Easier audit trail for card transactions vs. cash

categories.name: Competitive / Strategic
ideas: Follow industry trend — all other airlines are evaluating the switch
Alignment with competitor Phoenix Air reduces competitive differentiation risk
Signals modernity and operational efficiency to customers and investors

categories.name: Potential New Costs / Risks to Flag
ideas: Wi-Fi or connectivity cost to process card transactions in-flight
Increased fraud risk with card-only transactions
Potential customer dissatisfaction among the minority who prefer cash
Regulatory risk if cash acceptance becomes mandated

recommendation: Wildcat Wings should switch to a card-only system for in-flight food and beverage purchases.

Financially, the $35/flight revenue loss from cash-only customers is exactly offset by $35/flight in overhead savings from eliminating cash management operations — but the overhead savings drop directly to the bottom line while revenue losses only partially affect profit, making the switch financially favorable.
Operationally, card-only accelerates payment collection from 31 days to 24 hours, improving cash flow and enabling better use of working capital.
Strategically, switching aligns Wildcat Wings with the direction of the industry and reduces operational complexity.
risks: Loss of revenue from the ~1/3 of cash customers who will not switch (approximately $35/flight)
Increased fraud exposure from card transactions
Connectivity/Wi-Fi costs to process transactions in-flight
Potential reputational risk or regulatory backlash if any jurisdiction mandates cash acceptance
next_steps: Pilot the card-only program on a subset of routes to validate the 1/3 cash-customer attrition assumption
Negotiate with the merchant services provider to reduce the 2% card processing fee given higher volume
Develop a plan to redeploy or transition the 7 cash management employees per airport
Evaluate investment options for the working capital freed up by faster payment collection
